one_line: Google AI Edge on running small Gemma models on-device via LiteRT-LM, the on-device agent-skills pattern (progressive disclosure, constrained tool calls), and fine-tuning tiny models with synthetic data.
summary: Cormac Brick (Google AI Edge) gives a state-of-the-art tour of on-device LLMs. He splits models into system-level (2-5B, built into the OS) and in-app "tiny" models (under 1B), and argues tiny models need fine-tuning for production reliability. He covers the Gemma 4 E2B/E4B models, which add built-in function calling and thinking, and their memory tricks. The core of the talk is an on-device agent-skills system in the AI Edge Gallery app: a one-line skill description sits in the prompt, the model loads a skill's full instructions on demand, and a small set of primitives (load skill, run JS, run intent) runs it. He describes a tiny-model playbook: synthetic data from a large model, fine-tuning a small Gemma derivative, quantization, and shipping one LiteRT-LM file across CPU/GPU, with AOT compilation for NPUs. The last part shows the offline dictation app Eloquent, built from modular ASR, personalization and text-polish models. Most numbers are vendor self-reports from internal evals. The talk is partly product showcase, but it contains concrete engineering patterns.

key_ideas.idea: Two deployment trends: system-level gen AI (2-5B models built into the OS) and in-app tiny models (under 1B) shipped with the app for wide device reach.
key_ideas.detail: System models are customized by prompting or skills. Tiny models are customized per task and aim for reach across all devices, not just premium phones.

key_ideas.idea: Below roughly 500M parameters, the speaker says fine-tuning is needed to reach production reliability. Above that, general prompting can work better.
key_ideas.detail: He says the 500M line is his team's experience, and that a single narrow task fine-tuned on a small model can reach strong performance.

key_ideas.idea: Agent skills work on small on-device models because of progressive disclosure: only one-line skill descriptions sit in context, and full instructions load only when the model chooses a skill.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker contrasts this with MCP, where all function details are loaded up front. Less context matters a lot for small models with weaker long-context reasoning.

key_ideas.idea: Constrained decoding is applied only to tool-call output and limited to the finite set of valid tools, which gives small models stronger guardrails.
key_ideas.detail: He says this helped a lot for the 2B model, and matters less as models get larger.

key_ideas.idea: Skills are built with coding agents. The team's favorite pattern was asking Gemini CLI or Claude Code to write a skill from docs and examples, then testing it on a phone over ADB.
key_ideas.detail: Of about 80 team skills, the speaker says more than half were vibe-coded at first. Community skills are collected through GitHub discussions and promoted into the app.

key_ideas.idea: Multi-skill use works across turns (one skill per turn). Skill stacking inside a single prompt works only when the prompt is very explicit, and its limits are still being explored.
key_ideas.detail: The speaker says the Gemma models were not specifically trained for the skill structure. The skill structure came after the model was tested.

key_ideas.idea: Tiny-model playbook: a large cloud model generates synthetic data, a small base model is fine-tuned on it, then it is quantized and shipped. Modular small models are preferred over one large model in the app.
key_ideas.detail: The Eloquent app splits speech recognition, a personalization word-bias list and a text-polish LLM. The split makes the pipeline easier to debug and lets models be reused. Scale of synthetic data mentioned is low millions to tens of millions of examples.

key_ideas.idea: Memory footprint: E2B/E4B keep about 2B/4B parameters resident. The per-layer embedding tables are memory-mapped and only the rows needed for each token are read.
key_ideas.detail: This is why the models are called effective-2B and effective-4B. The speaker says the KV cache per input token was also optimized for edge.

techniques.name: Progressive disclosure for skills
techniques.how: Put a one-line description of each skill in the system prompt. Give the model a load_skill tool that returns the full SKILL.md (instructions, tool calls, scripts) only when it picks a skill. Trigger metadata is always loaded; the body is loaded on demand.
techniques.when: Many tools or skills, a small model with a limited context window, or when token efficiency and reliability matter more than having every detail in context.

techniques.name: Three-primitive orchestrator
techniques.how: Build a small set of primitives (load_skill, run_js, run_intent) and let the model compose them. Skills can be local JavaScript, Android intents, or web API calls that need a user-provided API key.
techniques.when: Extending an on-device assistant without fine-tuning, with a low barrier for third parties to add skills.

techniques.name: Constrained decoding scoped to tool calls
techniques.how: Enable constrained decoding only for the output span that is a tool call, and constrain it to the finite set of tool names that are valid for the current turn instead of generic JSON.
techniques.when: Small models (around 2B) doing function calling where the tool set is finite and known.

techniques.name: Synthetic data then fine-tune then quantize
techniques.how: Use a strong cloud LLM to generate a large synthetic dataset for one narrow task, fine-tune a small base model on it (the speaker says low millions to tens of millions of examples), then quantize and ship as a single file.
techniques.when: A narrow feature that must run on a wide range of devices offline and at low cost.

techniques.name: Modular pipeline of small models
techniques.how: Split a voice product into separate models: ASR, a custom vocabulary/bias list (names, technical terms) and a text-polish LLM (remove filler words, apply the vocabulary, handle self-corrections). Each model can be inspected and reused.
techniques.when: Offline dictation or transcription where custom terms matter and the team wants to debug each stage.

techniques.name: LoRA hot-swap on one base model
techniques.how: Keep one base model resident and fine-tune small LoRA adapters per task (about 8-100 MB each, depending on rank). Swap adapters at runtime without reloading the base model.
techniques.when: Embedded or robotics devices with several narrow tasks and limited memory.

techniques.name: Skill testing loop with a coding agent and a device
techniques.how: Give a coding agent the docs, example skills and a connected phone (ADB). Ask it to write the skill, run it on the device, check the behaviour, and iterate.
techniques.when: Fast prototyping of agent skills or tools that must run in a real app.

techniques.name: Build-once, deploy-everywhere model file with AOT for NPU
techniques.how: Export a PyTorch model to a single LiteRT-LM file (tokenizer included) that runs on CPU/GPU via JIT. For NPU, run a vendor compiler plugin ahead of time to produce a device-specific artifact. The same runtime API is used for both.
techniques.when: Shipping one model to many platforms, and adding NPU acceleration where the hardware supports it.

numbers.claim: Function Gemma (270M) on 10 Android voice-to-function-call tasks: about 85-90% reliability on internal eval.
Mobile-actions fine-tune on 10 functions: eight simple functions above 93%; two harder functions pulled the average to about 86%.
Fine-tuning improved small models by about 20-40 points on the team's evals.
Models under 500M parameters need fine-tuning for production reliability (speaker's experience).
Tiny models are defined as under 1B parameters; system-level OS models are typically 2-5B.
E2B needs about 2B parameters resident in RAM and E4B about 4B; the rest is per-layer embeddings that are memory-mapped.
E2B on a high-end Android phone GPU and on a MacBook: thousands of tokens per second (prefill and decode). On a Raspberry Pi: about 133 tokens per second.
E2B and E4B support context up to 32K tokens; the larger Gemma 4 models support 128K. The Gallery app defaults to about 8K-12K for performance.
Gemma 4 E2B/E4B are multimodal (audio, image, text) and released under Apache 2.0, the first Gemma release under that license.
Team built about 80 skills for the Gallery app; more than half were vibe-coded at first.
All Gallery skill demos ran on the 4B model; 2B also works, with more variability for complex skills.
FastVLM (Apple, 500M) runs with Qualcomm hardware acceleration on an S25; about 250-260 MB extra in the app if 4-bit quantized (speaker's estimate, not done in the demo).
EmbeddingGemma is about 300M parameters and is intended for on-device RAG embeddings.
Synthetic data scale for tiny-model fine-tuning: low millions to tens of millions of examples.
LoRA adapters for the 2B model are about 8-100 MB depending on rank, and the runtime can hot-swap them without reloading the base.

hot_takes: For models under about 500M parameters, prompting is not enough for production; fine-tune.
Skills are a better extension path than fine-tuning for the 2B/4B Gemma models, but tiny models should be fine-tuned.
Most of the team's skills were vibe-coded with coding agents at first, and this lowered the barrier to extending a model.
On-device, one of the most valuable things is a narrow, fine-tuned, modular model pipeline rather than one large model.

relevance.why: AgentOS L2B targets one RTX 5090 with vLLM, and the talk's progressive-disclosure skill loader and constrained tool-name decoding are directly applicable to a small-model local tier and to SkillForge's skill format.
relevance.action: Prototype a load_skill-style layer for SkillForge: put only one-line skill descriptions in the system prompt, load full SKILL.md on demand, and measure prompt tokens and tool-call accuracy against the current full-description approach on a 4B-class local model.

relevance.why: ProsHarness wraps Claude Code and ranks skills. The talk's skill-writing loop (agent writes a skill, tests it on a device, iterates) and load-on-demand pattern are relevant to skill ranking and validation.
relevance.action: Read the talk's skill-spec and load-skill approach to check whether ProsHarness skill ranking should gate skills on an automated run-and-verify step before they are ranked.

relevance.why: The synthetic-data-then-fine-tune loop for a narrow task, and constrained decoding limited to a finite tool set, apply to cheap-model (Haiku) pipelines and to structured extraction work.
relevance.action: For a narrow cheap-model task in the entity-resolution or extraction pipeline, generate synthetic labelled data with a larger model, fine-tune a small model, and measure the gain on a held-out set; also try restricting output to the valid label set for constrained decoding.
